claim: ParABS partition systems ensure stable inheritance of many bacterial chromosomes and low-copy-number plasmids.
source: Three-component ParABS partition systems ensure stable inheritance of many bacterial chromosomes and low-copy-number plasmids.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ParABS systems in the abstract.

claim: ParA localizes to the nucleoid through its ATP-dependent nonspecific DNA-binding activity.
source: ParA localizes to the nucleoid through its ATP-dependent nonspecific DNA-binding activity
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Centromere-like parS-DNA and ParB form partition complexes that activate ParA-ATPase to drive the system dynamics.
source: centromere-like parS-DNA and ParB form partition complexes that activate ParA-ATPase to drive the system dynamics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ParABS systems cited in the introduction.

claim: parSpSM with four or more contiguous ParBpSM-binding sequence repeats is required to assemble a stable ParApSM-ParBpSM complex.
source: We show that parSpSM with four or more contiguous ParBpSM-binding sequence repeats is required to assemble a stable ParApSM-ParBpSM complex
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 1-5.

claim: parSpSM with four or more contiguous ParBpSM-binding sequence repeats efficiently activates the ParApSM-ATPase.
source: parSpSM with four or more contiguous ParBpSM-binding sequence repeats is required to assemble a stable ParApSM-ParBpSM complex and efficiently activate the ParApSM-ATPase
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ATPase assay data in Figure 1.

claim: Disruption of the contiguity of the parSpSM sequence array destabilizes the ParApSM-ParBpSM complex.
source: Disruption of the contiguity of the parSpSM sequence array destabilizes the ParApSM-ParBpSM complex
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3-4.

claim: Disruption of the contiguity of the parSpSM sequence array prevents efficient ATPase activation.
source: Disruption of the contiguity of the parSpSM sequence array destabilizes the ParApSM-ParBpSM complex and prevents efficient ATPase activation.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase assay data in Figure 1C.

claim: ATP-activated ParA dimers bind nonspecific DNA and localize to the nucleoid in vivo.
source: ATP-activated ParA dimers bind nonspecific DNA (nsDNA) and localize to the nucleoid in vivo (Ebersbach and Gerdes, 2001; Ebersbach and Gerdes, 2004; Pratto et al., 2008; Ringgaard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: ParB proteins fall into two structurally unrelated groups: dimeric helix-turn-helix (HTH) and dimeric ribbon-helix-helix (RHH) DNA-binding proteins.
source: ParB proteins fall into two structurally unrelated groups, dimeric helix-turn-helix (HTH), and dimeric ribbon-helix-helix (RHH) DNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ParB protein classification.

claim: HTH-ParBs bind site-specifically to their cognate parS sequences and spread many kilobase pairs into the DNA neighboring the parS sites.
source: HTH-ParBs have been shown to bind not only site-specifically to their cognate parS sequences but also to spread many kilobase pairs into the DNA neighboring the parS sites (Murray et al., 2006; Graham et al., 2014; Soh et al., 2019; Rodionov et al., 1999; Lynch and Wang, 1995; Breier and Grossman, 2007; Jalal et al., 2020; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: HTH-ParBs form large PCs containing many ParB molecules bound to condensed DNA around parS.
source: Therefore, they form large PCs containing many ParB molecules bound to condensed DNA around parS
evidence: This is inferred from the spreading behavior of HTH-ParBs and supported by citations.

claim: ParB spreading activity is essential for HTH-ParB partition function.
source: ParB spreading activity is essential for their partition function (Rodionov et al., 1999; Debaugny et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RHH-ParB does not spread beyond parS site judged by the absence of ParB-mediated silencing of parS-proximal gene expression.
source: In contrast, RHH-ParB does not spread beyond parS site judged by the absence of ParB-mediated silencing of parS-proximal gene expression (J. C. Alonso, unpublished observation)
evidence: This is supported by unpublished observations.

claim: RHH-ParBs interact with their cognate ParA proteins via their N-terminus.
source: but like HTH-ParBs, they interact with their cognate ParA proteins via their N-terminus (Radnedge et al., 1998; Figge et al., 2003; Barillà et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RHH-ParB proteins control the expression of the proteins involved in the partition system and plasmid copy number control by binding parS sites which overlaps promoters of their genes.
source: RHH-ParB proteins also control the expression of the proteins involved in the partition system and plasmid copy number control by binding parS sites, which overlaps promoters of their genes (de la Hoz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ParA–ParB interaction leads to activation of the ParA-ATPase, which is most efficient in the presence of nsDNA and parS DNA.
source: ParA–ParB interaction leads to activation of the ParA-ATPase, which is most efficient in the presence of nsDNA and parS DNA (Ah-Seng et al., 2009; Chu et al., 2019; Pratto et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ParA-ATPase activation leads to dissociation of ParA from nsDNA.
source: ParA–ParB interaction leads to activation of the ParA-ATPase, which is most efficient in the presence of nsDNA and parS DNA (Ah-Seng et al., 2009; Chu et al., 2019; Pratto et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2021) and leads to dissociation of ParA from nsDNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The common results of most ParABS systems in vivo appear to be the establishment of equidistant distribution of two or more PCs along the nucleoid(s) so that at cell division each daughter cell inherits at least one copy of the plasmid DNA.
source: The common results of most systems in vivo appear to be the establishment of equidistant distribution of two or more PCs along the nucleoid(s) so that at cell division each daughter cell inherits at least one copy of the plasmid DNA (Sengupta et al., 2010; Ringgaard et al., 2009; Lioy et al., 2015; McLeod et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A diffusion-ratchet mechanism of the ParABS partition was proposed where the driving force for the DNA-cargo motion is generated by a propagating nucleoid-bound ParA distribution gradient.
source: a diffusion-ratchet mechanism of the ParABS partition was proposed. Here, the driving force for the DNA-cargo motion is generated by a propagating nucleoid-bound ParA distribution gradient (Vecchiarelli et al., 2010; Hwang et al., 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2013; Vecchiarelli et al., 2014; Sugawara and Kaneko, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work proposing the model.

claim: Each ParBpSM dimer binds one copy of the 7 bp parSpSM consensus sequence.
source: Each ParBpSM dimer binds one copy of the 7 bp parSpSM consensus sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ParBpSM binding.

claim: The affinity of ParBpSM for a single repeat is low, while two dimers bind with high affinity to two direct or inverted repeats forming dimers of dimers.
source: However, the affinity for a single repeat is low, while two dimers bind with high affinity to two direct (→→) or inverted (→←) repeats forming dimers of dimers (de la Hoz et al., 2004; Weihofen et al., 2006; Welfle et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Within the structures of ParBpSM-parSpSM complexes, DNA does not show significant curvature.
source: Within the structures of these ParBpSM-parSpSM complexes, DNA does not show significant curvature
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: Full-size parSpSM-ParBpSM complexes could be modeled as nearly straight DNA wrapped by left-handed spiral arrangement of ParBpSM dimers.
source: full-size parSpSM-ParBpSM complexes could be modeled as nearly straight DNA wrapped by left-handed spiral arrangement of ParBpSM dimers (Weihofen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural modeling work.

claim: Atomic force microscopy images of the complex involving seven parSpSM consensus sequence repeats supported its straight arrangement and the lack of spreading.
source: Atomic force microscopy images of the complex involving seven parSpSM consensus sequence repeats supported its straight arrangement and the lack of spreading (Pratto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to AFM imaging work.

claim: ParApSM, unlike most other ParAs, forms dimers in solution in the absence of ATP.
source: ParApSM, unlike most other ParAs, forms dimers in solution in the absence of ATP (Pratto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ParApSM undergoes a conformational transition upon binding ATP that increases its affinity for nsDNA.
source: Like other ParAs, it also undergoes a conformational transition upon binding ATP that increases its affinity for nsDNA (Soberón et al., 2011; Pratto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the ATP-bound form, ParApSM binds nsDNA forming limited size patches containing several ParApSM dimers at random location, instead of individual dimers independently distributed on the nsDNA.
source: In the ATP-bound form, ParApSM has been shown to bind nsDNA forming limited size patches containing several ParApSM dimers at random location, instead of individual dimers independently distributed on the nsDNA (Pratto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the presence of parSpSM DNA and ParBpSM, several parSpSM-ParBpSM mini-filaments and ParApSM-nsDNA patches appeared to bind together to form large protein-DNA complexes bridging multiple DNA molecules.
source: In the presence of parSpSM DNA and ParBpSM, several parSpSM-ParBpSM mini-filaments and ParApSM-nsDNA patches appeared to bind together to form large protein-DNA complexes bridging multiple DNA molecules (Pratto et al., 2008; Pratto et al., 2009; Soberón et al., 2011; Lioy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The turnover rate of ParApSM ATPase alone is very low at 37°C (0.9 ± 0.1 ATP/ParA-dimer/h, N = 3).
source: The turnover rate of ParApSM ATPase alone is very low at 37°C (0.9 ± 0.1 ATP/ParA-dimer/h, N = 3; Figure 1A; no DNA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the presence of saturating concentration of double-stranded DNA without parSpSM sequence, no significant rate change of ParApSM ATPase was observed compared to ParApSM alone.
source: In the presence of a saturating concentration of double-stranded DNA (40 μg/ml pBR322 plasmid DNA plus 23–38 μg/ml double-stranded oligonucleotide with or without parSpSM sequence), to which ATP-ParApSM dimers can bind to support ATPase activation by ParBpSM (see below), no significant rate change was observed (1.0 ± 0.1 h–1, N = 46, Figure 1A, pool of all measurements at [ParBpSM] = 0).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ParApSM ATP hydrolysis was stimulated up to ~20-fold (kcat = 20.5 ± 2.9 h–1, N = 7) in the presence of ParBpSM and oligonucleotide duplex DNA containing seven parSpSM heptad-sequence-repeats (7R-parSpSM).
source: ParApSM ATP hydrolysis was stimulated up to ~20-fold (kcat = 20.5 ± 2.9 h–1, N = 7) in the presence of ParBpSM and oligonucleotide duplex DNA containing one of the native arrangements containing seven parSpSM heptad-sequence-repeats (7R-parSpSM, →→←→→←←) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The stimulation of ParApSM ATPase by ParBpSM and 7R-parSpSM approached saturation around 2 μM ParBpSM at varying ParApSM concentrations.
source: The stimulation approached saturation around 2 μM ParBpSM at varying ParApSM concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When the parSpSM DNA fragment was replaced with one having a scrambled sequence, ParBpSM stimulated ParApSM ATPase activity only to 2.4 ± 1.1 h–1 even in the presence of 8 μM ParBpSM.
source: In contrast, when the parSpSM DNA fragment was replaced with one having a scrambled sequence, ParBpSM stimulated ParApSM ATPase activity only to 2.4 ± 1.1 h–1 even in the presence of 8 μM ParBpSM that should have allowed non-parSpSM DNA binding (N = 3*) (Figure 1A, scram).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A low level of ParApSM ATPase stimulation was observed with ParBpSM1-27 peptide, which lacked the DNA-binding and dimerization domains.
source: Similarly, a low level of ParApSM ATPase stimulation was observed with ParBpSM1-27 peptide, which lacked the DNA-binding and dimerization domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Full ParApSM-ATPase stimulation by ParBpSM requires specific parSpSM interactions.
source: These results demonstrated that full ParApSM-ATPase stimulation by ParBpSM requires specific parSpSM interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing parSpSM vs scrambled DNA.

claim: The low parSpSM-independent ATPase stimulation was not detected in the absence of DNA.
source: Even the low parSpSM-independent ATPase stimulation was not detected in the absence of DNA (Figure 1A, no DNA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The low-level ATPase stimulation by non-parSpSM-binding ParBpSM1-27 peptide was not detected without DNA.
source: Similarly, the low-level ATPase stimulation by non-parSpSM-binding ParBpSM1-27 peptide was not detected without DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ParApSM-nsDNA binding is required for the ATPase activation by ParBpSM.
source: We conclude ParApSM-nsDNA binding is required for the ATPase activation by ParBpSM, as reported for ParAF ATPase activation by ParBF (Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to similar findings in another system.

claim: In the absence of nsDNA, excess ParBpSM relative to the concentration of 7R-parSpSM in the reaction inhibited ATPase stimulation, presumably competing with ParApSM for parSpSM DNA binding.
source: Consistently, in the absence of nsDNA, excess ParBpSM relative to the concentration of 7R-parSpSM in the reaction inhibited ATPase stimulation, presumably competing with ParApSM for parSpSM DNA binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Efficient ATPase stimulation was observed when 6R, 5R, or 4R parSpSM was added along ParBpSM.
source: Efficient ATPase stimulation was observed when 6R (→←→→←←), 5R (→→→←←), or 4R (→→←←) was added along ParBpSM (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No significant difference in ATPase stimulation was observed among 5R, 6R, or 7R parSpSM; both half-saturation concentrations and the apparent kcat were comparable.
source: No significant difference was observed among 5R, 6R, or 7R; both half-saturation concentrations and the apparent kcat were comparable (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ParBpSM-4R-parSpSM induced similar rates of ParApSM ATP hydrolysis as 5R, 6R, or 7R, but a significantly higher concentration was required for full stimulation.
source: ParBpSM-4R-parSpSM also induced similar rates of ParApSM ATP hydrolysis, but a significantly higher concentration was required for full stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Different heptad orientation arrangements of 4R-parSpSM (→→←→ and →→→→) stimulated ParApSM ATPase to a similar extent.
source: Different heptad orientation arrangements of 4R-parSpSM (→→←→ and →→→→) stimulated ParApSM ATPase to a similar extent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 3R-, 2R-, and 1R-parSpSM were poor cofactors for ParBpSM-dependent ATPase stimulation (apparent kcat = 3.2–3.6 ± 1.3–2.1 h–1, N = 4–7*), not significantly different from the scrambled sequence DNA.
source: In contrast, 3R- (→→←), 2R- (→←), and 1R- (→) parSpSM were poor cofactors for ParBpSM-dependent ATPase stimulation (apparent kcat = 3.2–3.6 ± 1.3–2.1 h–1, N = 4–7*, Figure 1A), not significantly different from the scrambled sequence DNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 3R-parSpSM fragments with different repeat arrangements behaved similarly to each other in ATPase stimulation.
source: 3R-parSpSM fragments with different repeat arrangements behaved similarly to each other (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ATPase stimulation by parSpSM DNA with 1–3 parSpSM repeats appeared to saturate at around 2 μM ParBpSM.
source: The ATPase stimulation by parSpSM DNA with 1–3 parSpSM repeats also appeared to saturate at around 2 μM ParBpSM
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: ParBpSM bound 3R, 4R DNA fragments of different sequence orientation combinations, or a 10R DNA fragment with roughly similar affinity that was >50-fold higher than nsDNA or 1R DNA.
source: Previously it has been shown that ParBpSM bound 3R, 4R DNA fragments of different sequence orientation combinations, or a 10R DNA fragment with roughly similar affinity that was >50-fold higher than nsDNA or 1R DNA (de la Hoz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ParBpSM binding was similarly strong for 4R and 3R duplex DNA (KD ~ 17 nM) and weak for nsDNA (KD ~ 1 μM).
source: We confirmed that ParBpSM binding was similarly strong for 4R and 3R duplex DNA (KD ~ 17 nM) and weak for nsDNA (KD ~ 1 μM, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The affinity of ParBpSM for the 3R-parSpSM DNA is not limiting the ParApSM ATPase stimulation.
source: Therefore, the affinity of ParBpSM for the 3R-parSpSM DNA is not limiting the ParApSM ATPase stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding affinity data.

claim: parSpSM-DNA fragment size was not a significant factor for the ATPase stimulation efficiency.
source: We tested longer 3R-parSpSM DNA fragments containing an additional non-parSpSM heptamer sequence (non-consensus, nc) (3R-1nc) and confirmed that parSpSM-DNA fragment size was not a significant factor for the ATPase stimulation efficiency (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ParApSM ATP turnover is fine-tuned by the structural arrangement of the ParBpSM and parSpSM within the PC.
source: These results suggested that ParApSM ATP turnover is fine-tuned by the structural arrangement of the ParBpSM and parSpSM within the PC.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing dependence on repeat number and arrangement.

claim: ParBpSM assembles as a left-handed spiral to wrap parSpSM DNA without significantly distorting the DNA backbone geometry.
source: ParBpSM assembles as a left-handed spiral to wrap parSpSM DNA without significantly distorting the DNA backbone geometry (Weihofen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: After approximately four repeats, ParBpSM dimers would make a full turn around parSpSM, positioning themselves on the same face of the nucleoprotein filament.
source: implying that after approximately four repeats, ParBpSM dimers would make a full turn around parSpSM, positioning themselves on the same face of the nucleoprotein filament.
evidence: This is inferred from the helical structure of the ParBpSM-parSpSM complex.

claim: The 3R-1nc-3R-parSpSM fragments showed only slightly higher stimulation (kcat = 8.3 ± 3.5 h–1, N = 8*) compared to the single 3R-parSpSM fragment.
source: The 3R-1nc-3R-parSpSM fragments showed only slightly higher stimulation (kcat = 8.3 ± 3.5 h–1, N = 8*) compared to the single 3R-parSpSM fragment
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 3R-2nc-3R parSpSM was functionally indistinguishable from the single 3R-parSpSM fragment.
source: and the 3R-2nc-3R was functionally indistinguishable from the single 3R-parSpSM fragment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Disrupted 6R-parSpSM fragments are unable to recover the full stimulation of ParApSM ATPase activity.
source: We conclude that disrupted 6R-parSpSM fragments are unable to recover the full stimulation of ParApSM ATPase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on gapped parSpSM fragments.

claim: The ParBpSM-ParApSM interactions differ when ParBpSM dimers are bound to ≥4 contiguous heptad repeats compared to ParBpSM dimers unbound to the repeats or bound to fewer or a disrupted array of heptad repeats.
source: These findings indicate that the ParBpSM-ParApSM interactions differ when ParBpSM dimers are bound to ≥4 contiguous heptad repeats compared to ParBpSM dimers unbound to the repeats or bound to fewer or a disrupted array of heptad repeats.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing functional differences.

claim: Significantly lower heptad consensus sequence concentrations of the 7R-parSpSM DNA fragment compared to ParBpSM dimers were sufficient for ATPase activation.
source: Contrary to our expectation, significantly lower heptad consensus sequence concentrations of the 7R-parSpSM DNA fragment compared to ParBpSM dimers (B2) were sufficient for ATPase activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At any given time, less than half of the ParBpSM dimers need to be in complex with 7R-parSpSM to exert full ATPase activation.
source: Thus, assuming most of the ParBpSM molecules in our preparations are active, it appears that at any given time, less than half of the ParBpSM dimers need to be in complex with 7R-parSpSM to exert full ATPase activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the substoichiometric requirement of parSpSM relative to ParBpSM.

claim: ParApSM-GFP ATPase activity stimulation by ParBpSM and 7R-parS was comparable to wild-type ParApSM.
source: Stimulation of ParApSM-GFP ATPase activity by ParBpSM and 7R-parS was comparable to wild-type ParApSM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ParBpSM-Alexa647 (1% labeled) in the absence of ParApSM accumulated on the DNA-carpet reaching a density of ~3000 ± 500 dimers/μm2 after 15 min of constant flow.
source: ParBpSM-Alexa647 in the absence of ParApSM accumulated on the DNA-carpet reaching a density of ~3000 ± 500 dimers/μm2 after 15 min of constant flow (5 μl/min) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When the sample solution was switched to a buffer without protein, most ParBpSM rapidly dissociated with kinetics that can be fitted to a double-exponential function (koff-fast = 5.1 ± 0.7 min–1 [73%], koff-slow = 0.11 ± 0.04 min–1, N = 3).
source: When the sample solution was switched to a buffer without protein, most ParBpSM rapidly dissociated with kinetics that can be fitted to a double-exponential function (koff-fast = 5.1 ± 0.7 min–1 [73%], koff-slow = 0.11 ± 0.04 min–1, N = 3; all koffs reported in this study represent apparent pseudo-first order rate constants) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ParApSM-GFP preincubated with ATP and Mg2+ reached a saturation density on the nsDNA-carpet of 4.25 (±0.06) × 104 dimers/μm2 (N = 4*).
source: ParApSM-GFP preincubated with ATP and Mg2+ reached a saturation density on the nsDNA-carpet of 4.25 (±0.06) × 104 dimers/μm2 (N = 4*)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the absence of ATP, less than 1000 dimers/μm2 of ParApSM bound to the nsDNA-carpet.
source: whereas in the absence of ATP, less than 1000 dimers/μm2 of ParApSM bound to the nsDNA-carpet (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A small fraction of ParApSM-GFP (less than ~5%) dissociated within ~1 min and the remainder dissociated slowly with koff of <0.013 min–1 (N = 3) when washed with ATP-containing buffer.
source: A small fraction of ParApSM-GFP (less than ~5%) dissociated within ~1 min and the remainder dissociated slowly with koff of <0.013 min–1 (N = 3, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The addition of competitor nsDNA (71 nM scrambled 55 bp duplex DNA) in the wash buffer slightly increased the koff of majority (~93%) fraction of ParApSM-GFP (koff = 0.075 ± 0.001 min–1, N = 3).
source: The addition of competitor nsDNA (71 nM scrambled 55 bp duplex DNA) in the wash buffer slightly increased the koff of majority (~93%) fraction of ParApSM-GFP (koff = 0.075 ± 0.001 min–1, N = 3), perhaps in part by competing with rebinding of ParApSM-GFP-ATP to the nsDNA-carpet (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: When 1 μM ParBpSM was added to the wash buffer without competitor nsDNA, koff of ParApSM-GFP from nsDNA-carpet reached 0.17 ± 0.01 min–1 (N = 4).
source: When 1 μM ParBpSM (unlabeled or 1% Alexa647 labeled) was added to the wash buffer without competitor nsDNA, koff of ParApSM-GFP from nsDNA-carpet reached 0.17 ± 0.01 min–1 (N = 4, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ParApSM-GFP dissociation from the nsDNA-carpet was accelerated when wash solution contained 71 nM 7R-parSpSM DNA and 1 μM ParBpSM (koff = 1.97 ± 0.09) after a brief period of initial slower dissociation rate.
source: ParApSM-GFP dissociation from the nsDNA-carpet was accelerated when wash solution contained 71 nM 7R-parSpSM DNA (0.5 μM of the consensus sequence repeat) and 1 μM ParBpSM (koff = 1.97 ± 0.09) after a brief period of initial slower dissociation rate (see below for details) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The koff of ParApSM-GFP with 7R-parSpSM and ParBpSM was ~12 or ~26-fold higher compared to ParBpSM or nsDNA wash, respectively.
source: This was ~12 or ~26-fold higher koff compared to ParBpSM or nsDNA wash, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: 4R-parSpSM DNA supported accelerated ParApSM-GFP release by ParBpSM, but 3R-parSpSM DNA did not.
source: Similarly, 4R-parSpSM DNA supported accelerated ParApSM-GFP release by ParBpSM, but 3R-parSpSM DNA did not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The results of ParApSM dissociation from nsDNA-carpet paralleled those of ATPase assays, solidifying the notion that a functional parSpSM must carry four copies of ParBpSM dimer-binding sequence repeats.
source: The results paralleled those shown in Figure 1A solidifying the notion that a functional parSpSM must carry four copies of ParBpSM dimer-binding sequence repeats.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results of Figures 1A and 2B.

claim: Upon switching the flow to the washing solution without parSpSM, ParBpSM bound to the ParApSM-bound nsDNA-carpet to a peak density of ~3000 dimers/μm2 and then quickly decreased to a plateau density of ~2000 dimers/μm2.
source: Upon switching the flow to the washing solution without parSpSM, ParBpSM bound to the ParApSM-bound nsDNA-carpet to a peak density of ~3000 dimers/μm2 and then quickly decreased to a plateau density of ~2000 dimers/μm2 (Figure 3Ad).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Ad.

claim: The initial overshoot of ParBpSM binding appeared to roughly coincide with the fast dissociation phase of ParApSM.
source: The initial overshoot of ParBpSM binding appeared to roughly coincide with the fast dissociation phase of ParApSM.
evidence: This is observed from the data in Figure 3Ad.

claim: During the subsequent slow dissociation of ParApSM, ParBpSM density on the nsDNA-carpet remained relatively constant with the protein ratio reaching ~1 after several min of washing with 1 μM ParBpSM.
source: During the subsequent slow dissociation of ParApSM, ParBpSM density on the nsDNA-carpet remained relatively constant with the protein ratio reaching ~1 after several min of washing with 1 μM ParBpSM (Figure 3Ad).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Ad.

claim: In the presence of 1 μM ParBpSM and 7R-parSpSM in the wash solution, ParApSM-GFP release from the nsDNA-carpet took place in two phases.
source: In the presence of 1 μM ParBpSM and 7R-parSpSM in the wash solution, ParApSM-GFP release from the nsDNA-carpet took place in two phases (Figure 3Aa).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Aa.

claim: First, ParBpSM accumulated on the ParApSM-bound nsDNA-carpet to a density twofold or more in excess of the carpet-bound ParApSM, during which ParApSM dissociated from the nsDNA-carpet relatively slowly.
source: First, ParBpSM accumulated on the ParApSM-bound nsDNA-carpet to a density twofold or more in excess of the carpet-bound ParApSM. During this phase, ParApSM dissociated from the nsDNA-carpet relatively slowly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Aa.

claim: As the binding of ParBpSM stopped and began to quickly dissociate (koff = 2.4 ± 0.1 min–1, N = 5), ParApSM dissociation also accelerated to a higher rate (koff = 1.8 ± 0.05 min–1, N = 5).
